## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.
raw_comment: I noticed some really interesting things about certain groups of Asian immigrants, such as the clustering of Indonesian immigrants in Montana and how most Burmese immigrants settled in the Midwest. I also noticed that most Asian immigrants lived in the Western parts of the United States, which makes sense, however Oregon seems to have significantly less Asian immigrants than California and Seattle. I wonder if they could have represented the data differently, as I found that having the visualization be based of whether or not the specific group makes up 0.5% of the population doesn't really represent how many people from that group live there, as some places may be just below the threshold and not show at all while others may be way above the threshold and still appear the same as every other place where the threshold is met. Furthermore, counties are different sizes, so bigger counties make it look like there's more Asian immigrants there when it's just the county being bigger.

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

raw_comment:
The Spread of Asians/Asian-Americans in the United States

It's interesting that the Asian population is more spread out. I think it's interesting that there's a larger Chinese community in California. This may be due to the gold rush that happened in the late 19th to early 20th century, where many Asians immigrated there to find opportunity for them and their families. I feel like it's also interesting that the Filipino population seems to be much less than the Chinese population. I think it's interesting that a lot of Vietemese people and Japanese are gathered in the midwest areas. I wonder why this may be so. Was there any specific event such as the gold rush that may have triggered a specific influx or decrease in these particular populations?

As an Asian American as well as Chinese-American, I think it's really fascinating to see the distribution of different Asian ethnicities spread across the United States. Many people tend to gravitate towards thinking about white races/European, but the map really showed how diverse populations in the States really are.

raw_comment:
1. It seems that the Asian population in this country is pretty spread out though it's interesting to see that the graphs show that people are more close to the coasts. Its also interesting haw mosts of the graphs shown spew to the west coast mostly California. Its also really interesting to me how Alaska has such a small population so this graph basically shows that a large amount of the Alasken population is Filipino. 

2. I wonder how come the Filipino population in the US is much less than say the Chinese population, yet the Filipino graph appears to be a lot more shaded. This makes me wonder if some Asian Ethnicities in the US will over time become a lot less prevalent. It's also interesting for me to see whether or not the distribution of groups will change over time. In 2030 will the Taiwanese graph look similar to the Korean one?

3. It's fascinating to me how the Asian population in has tripled in the past. Though only now are we just making advances like the first Asian Marvel Superhero. Though I am not Asian American it is very interesting how the different groups are spread out. As an Israeli-American person this graph makes me want to learn more about where I'm from and where Israeli American people are in this country. 

4. Lets Move Forward (A graph about the Major Asian group distribution in the US)

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

raw_comment:
I notice that the Asian population tends to be more dense in the east and west coast. On top of that, the Asian population seems to be less spread out, and more concentrated in certain area. There are around 205,000 Thai people in the USA, but a large portion of that population is in California (that goes for a lot of the other Asian groups as well). 

I wonder why there is such a large concentration of people in one spot, and if there is any sort of history behind why that is. I also wonder why so many Filipino people are in Alaska. Is there a story behind that as well?

While I am not an Asian-American, I do find it very interesting to see how different groups of people spread out across the state. This graph makes me want to look back on where I'm from, and see if there are dense populations of people from other places across the globe.

"Density and Diversity: The Asian Population Across the Country"

raw_comment:
1. I notice that some of the Asian populations are spread out across the country, while others are more densely populated to one side of the nation. For instance, the Filipino population tends to be more concentrated on the west coast, while the Indian population is more evenly spread out across the nation. As a Korean person living on the east coast, I notice that I am part of a seemingly smaller proportion compared to Koreans on the western side of the U.S. 

2. I wonder if certain Asian ethnicities will become more prevalent over time, while others become less prevalent. Also, I'd like to see how the distribution of certain groups will change over time – will they become more densely populated, or more spread out?

3. As an Asian American (specifically a Korean-American), I find it really interesting to see how the communities are distributed across the country. This data just goes to show how many Asian ethnicities and cultures there are, which is something many people forget about or tend to overlook. All of Asia should be represented, and I think this visual does a good job at highlighting a portion of the sheer diversity that's present in Asian culture.

4.Among us

raw_comment:
1. I notice that some of the Asian populations are spread out across the country, while others are more densely populated to one side of the nation. For instance, the Filipino population tends to be more concentrated on the west coast, while the Indian population is more evenly spread out across the nation. As a Korean person living on the east coast, I notice that I am part of a seemingly smaller proportion compared to Koreans on the western side of the U.S. 

2. I wonder if certain Asian ethnicities will become more prevalent over time, while others become less prevalent. Also, I'd like to see how the distribution of certain groups will change over time – will they become more densely populated, or more spread out?

3. As an Asian American (specifically a Korean-American), I find it really interesting to see how the communities are distributed across the country. This data just goes to show how many Asian ethnicities and cultures there are, which is something many people forget about or tend to overlook. All of Asia should be represented, and I think this visual does a good job at highlighting a portion of the sheer diversity that's present in Asian culture.

4. Asian Populations in the U.S. – A Distribution of Diversity

raw_comment:
My eyes were first drawn to the large shaded areas that can be found especially on the Chinese, Filipino, Korean, and Japanese population maps. However, this lead me to question why the Filipino map appeared to be shaded in more than the Chinese map when the Chinese population was greater by over 1 million. Thus, I suspected that the large shaded portions likely resulted from the counties in those states being less populated and thus having county lines that are drawn larger. I also noticed that a lot of the shaded areas for the larges Asian populations are in the areas where there are major cities on the east and west coasts.

I wonder what background context and events result in certain populations clustering around areas of interest such as Filipinos  in the mountain region and Alaska, the Japanese in Hawaii, and also how all of the smaller Asian populations came to gather in the few areas they show up on the map. I am curious about the shaded region at the very bottom of where California borders Nevada where it seems many Asian populations, including two of the smaller ones are gathered: Chinese, Korean, Thai, and Laotian.

This relates to me as an Asian-American, particularly one belonging to the largest group the Chinese, because it shows me just how immensely diverse the Asian racial group is. It's been fascinating observing where these different populations tend to gather and seeing where I fall.

Where do Asian Populations tend to Concentrate and Cluster in the US?

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

raw_comment:
I find it interesting that there are vast percentages of Filipino people in Alaska and Hawaii. At the same time, there are almost no other Asian groups in those areas except for the Japanese, who have a good amount in Hawaii. image_description:
## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

Thanks to all students who responded. Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: "How Major Asian Groups Are Dispersed in the Country" by Colleen of Academy of Saint Elizabeth in Morristown, New Jersey; "Asians in America: Scattered or Clustered Across the States" by S of Pennsylvania and “The Asian Population in America is Coasting” by Fiona and “Asians on the Map” by Erin, both of USA.

We encourage you to continue to post responses. Please check back by Friday, Jan. 28 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a Stat Nugget.

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The first observation I make is that all 16 of the maps are of the United States. I then take into account the headline: "Geographic distribution of major Asian groups" which leads me into my conclusion that this graph is displaying the various places different Asian decent people live in the United States. I also notice the fact that starting with Chinese people being the largest population number at 4.1 million, the graphs slowly start to show a trend from most to least ending with Indonesian at just 75,000 people. Additionally, after analyzing the maps i see that the Asian population is much more substantial in urban states like California or New York, but not nearly as much identified in the middle states like Montana. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder how they created this poll and how accurate it is. In addition, I wonder why this poll was created? Is it beneficial to see where Asian immigrants choose to reside? I also wonder if they come to the US for a certain state or job. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community in a variety of ways such as the Asian population around me. I can definitely say I know of many many Asian people in my life, and think they are quite prevalent in my county. 
Create a catchy headline.
"Understanding Geographical Diversity"

1. What do you notice?

I notice that a majority of the larger Asian groups tended to live closer to the West Coast, with their demographics being much more clustered in states such as California. I also notice there is a large population of Asian Groups settled by the North Coast, with states such as Massachusetts and New York being heavily populated.

This impacts me and my community because these graphs present me with a way of seeing the diversity not only in the country but in the local area as well. The graphs show me the different Asian Groups located in or around my area.

This graph demonstrates the 16 selected Asian groups and their population in the United States.

raw_comment: I noticed that the Chinese population is the highest Asian population in America. It shows that most of the Chinese population lives in the West. **Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

raw_comment:
I noticed that Chinese, Indian, and Filipino groups are the highest in the United States. Based on the maps, these three groups are also very spread out across the United States, but the Filipino population is a bit more condensed compared to the Indian and Chinese populations. Out of all of the maps, the most populated areas seem to be on the coasts, particularly near the two largest US cities: New York and Los Angeles. 

A few things I wonder are why these groups are choosing to settle on the coasts. Particularly because they are areas of living that are more costly. Another thing I'm wondering is why there are so many Filipinos in Alaska. In general, I'm also wondering why there are only around 4 million in the two highest groups. 

This graph relates to me and my community because the United States is trying to improve its diversity and racial equality. Having knowledge of different culture can improve American society and facilitate unity across different groups of people.

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.
raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s maps show where, in 2020, U.S. residents who self-identify as members of the 16 largest groups of Asian countries of origin live.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these maps and six other graphics plus much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.  Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Jan. 28 with moderation on Wednesday, Feb. 2.  The topic:  Cobalt!  Keep noticing and wondering!

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

raw_comment:
1. In each of these displayed graphs, the population of different Asian groups within in the US are shown using blue colored spots. It appears that the most condensed areas are the Far East and west, regardless of which ethnic groups asian people belong to. I noticed that the Chinese population is the largest group displayed, while Indonesia is the smallest. 

2. When did the Chinese population become the largest and why? Are these populations proportional to the amount of people in these ethnic groups around the world? Is there a reason that the majority of the Asian population in the US is either living on the far eat or west side of the country?

3. This relates to me and my community as I have learned more and more about Asian culture in the recent years. The importance of diversification has become much more prevalent and how embracing differences can bring people together. My school community is very diverse and offers great opportunities to learn about different cultures and where they came from.

4. From one side of the world to the other, where have Asian people migrated to?

raw_comment:
I first noticed that the Filipino map has the highest percentage of shaded areas in comparison with the other maps. This suggested to me, at first, that Filipinos have the highest population of Asian groups in the U.S. However, after taking a closer look at the numbers, I found that Chinese has the highest population. I figured that this irregularity is due to the low overall populations of western states like Utah, Nevada, and Alaska.

I wonder why certain Asian groups, like Chinese and Indian, have higher populations in the U.S. I also wonder why each group of Asian descent settles in different locations in the U.S.

This graph relates to my community because as we are increasing awareness in the U.S. about different cultures, it is important to be able to differentiate between continental cultures.

raw_comment:
I notice right away that the Filipino map has the most color and has a lot of large, saturated blobs, but interestingly their overall population is smaller than the Chinese and Indian populations. Another thing I noticed is that the distribution of Chinese and Indian people across America is very similar, especially on the east coast. It's also interesting how the majority of color resides on both the east and west coast, but less so in the middle. 

I wonder why it seems like only Chinese, Filipino, and Japanese people seem to make up more than 0.5% of the population in Hawaii. Although I understand why there are a lot of Filipinos, I wasn't aware of such a large Chinese and Japanese population there. 

This relates to me and my community because I am Chinese, and it's interesting to see how in my area, the amount of Chinese and some other Asian groups are relatively saturated.

- Indonesian population has the least population in the US

| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

Title: The Melting Pot of America 

What do you notice?
--> At first glance, it appears the Filipino population would consist of the highest population in America given the darker, larger blue clusters; however, the Chinese community has a very widespread population across all of America. 
--> In contrast to the widespread Chinese population, smaller populations tend to group in one region of America. For example,

--> I wonder if the 23andMe program has anything to do with the increase in the population of Asian identities in America. There have several, fairly recent companies that assist people in learning about their pedigree through DNA testing. If individuals who have no awareness of their Asian descent, take the test, then they may recently identify with their past. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
--> This graph can inspire us to learn more about Asian culture and what diversity can bring to America. For example, there may be new food shops, fashion inspiration, traditions, and more. Becomming more aware of Asian culture can help limit the risk of being culturally insensitive.

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

raw_comment:
(1) What I noticed first is that the highest concentration of Asians in America seems to be Chinese with a 4.1 million population. Not only that but from the plots it seems that there is a higher concentration of Chinese people on the East Coast.  There is a very low population of Indonesian people, only about 75,000 and they all seem to populate in the Montana area.

(2) I wonder why certain groups in the Asian community are drawn to a certain area. For example, why do Chinese people populate more on the East Coast than the West Coast or even the midwest?
 
(3) I come from a family of immigrants and when we first came to America we decided to move upstate because we already had family here. I wonder if this is the same for other immigrants. Where I'm from we also do have a very big Asian community and it's interesting to kind of see a visual graph that represents this.

(4) Asian Immigration in America

raw_comment:
Headline: Asian in America: What Are Their Choices?

I noticed that the Asian population is more spread across the whole state which differs from what I assumed it would be. Though I also noticed that some particular Asians tend to stay more grouped in the west rather than the east possibly because it would generally be warmer. I wondered why there would be so many Filipinos choosing to stay in Alaska. Also, following the previous question, I wonder what would be the cause of different Asian populations choosing certain states. Is it because of the climate? Financial issues? Or other outside factors? I also wonder what type of age are the population mentioning. If there isn’t any, I personally think it could be nice to have a specific description of what age of Asian population is in certain areas, such as international students, family, etc.

I think it personally relates to me because I am a Korean student but I live in Pennsylvania and it is interesting to see that most Korean population resides in California, west.

raw_comment:
The map that stands out the most is that of the Filipino community because they inhabit large pieces of the map, mostly on the west, in Alaska, and Hawaii. The Indian and Pakistani populations are mostly on the east coast, while Korean and Chinese populations are very similar with people on the east and west, but not in the middle. Japanese people are mostly in the west.

raw_comment: In this graph, I noticed that California seems to be the only state that has some sort of concentration. Noticings:
- the Chinese and Filipino populations are primarily on the west coast-- have more and larger blue spaces on the west than the east coast.
- only 16 maps (16 ethnicities) but 20 countries
- the only states on the west coast that have any Pakistani populations are California, Washington, and Nevada
- almost all ethnicities have a community/population that lives in California 
- people of a certain ethnicity seem to live in similar areas to each other
Wonders:
- does an ethnicity cover more than one country?
- does Chinese mean Han Chinese? or all Chinese? because Hmong are from china but separated as a different ethnic group in these maps
- what if your family came here before these countries were established? do you count as one of these ethnicities

- most of these ethnicities have a community and population in Washington (where we live)
- WA has a large port that has access to Asia and a large Asian population here, so we should be aware of the different ethnicities that live here as people are proud of their individual ethnicities
Titles:
- Asian Persuasion

raw_comment:
In this graph, I noticed that the main concentration of Asian populations in the US is concentrated on the West Coast. Specifically, Filipino, Japanese, and Korean populations seem to flourish on the West Coast. I think it is interesting the spread of settlement of major Asian groups falls directly on the coasts, but I also think it is important to note that some groups are shown in rater unpopulated areas. For example, Filipinos account for a significant population of Alaska. 

I wonder if this graph includes immigration or descendants from Asain families who were born in the United States. If so, how far back is the generation born in the original Asian country? I would also be interested to see this graph from a chronological standpoint. I wonder if the major areas of Asian settlement have shifted over time or if they were always in these states.

This relates to my community because a significant portion of my friends and classmates are Asian. I think it is really interesting to learn about the settlement of different population groups and see the increase in diversity across the country. 

A catchy headline is: The United States of America or Asia? - Asian Populations on the Rise!

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.
raw_comment: I am not surprised that the most populous Asian groups are concentrated on the West and Easts coasts, given that there are established pockets of those cultures for decades in this country. I am more surprised about the concentration of certain ethnicities/nationalities in more rural or remote parts of the country, such Filipinos in Alaska, Cambodians in Utah, and Burmese in South Dakota. I wonder if those more rural communities are related to the overall move to rural areas due to costs of living in the major urban areas. However, the map might be slightly misleading when it comes to those states. This map shows those groups as "area where each group makes up at least 0.5% of the total population." Due to the lower populations of those states, the representation of the distribution of those Asian populations will look larger, despite the actual number of Asians being lower than that of New York or Californai.

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

raw_comment:
Headline: 2020's Map of Several Seperate Asian Populations


I think it is interesting that the populations are mostly spread out, although there are small groups typically along the east coast and largely in California. I am very interested in the Filipino population in Alaska since I do not know much about Alaska. The Japanese population seems to reside around the west coast, in both the north and the south. I also wondered about how these are only showing at least .5% of the population which means that a city could have 1 in 200 people being Chinese, or it could be around 50 in 200 people being Chinese and this map would not represent the percent of the population that is above 0.5%.

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.

- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

raw_comment:
I notice that Asian populations are mostly located along the West Coast, but there are still some closer to the East coast. I also notice that certain populations are larger than others and located in different areas. 
I wonder if these populations include people of Asian descent, but born in the U.S., or only immigrants. raw_comment:
I notice that the majority of Asian heritage is on the coasts. Most don't live in the Midwest or the south. I also notice that the larger countries, such as China and India, have more people of Asian descent than the smaller countries, like Nepal and Indonesia.

I wonder why most people of Asian descent live on the coasts. I also wonder why most people of Chinese descent live in California. Is it because of the large mass of Chinese descent and places like Chinatown?

This relates to me and my community because our community is very diverse and there are many people in our school of Asian descent.

My catchy title for this graph would be "Asian Population Rising on the Coast"

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

raw_comment:
tice that the majority of Asian heritage lies on the East coast and West coast. There is less of an asian population within the midwest and south. However, most areas have clusters of asian populations on the West coast rather than being spread out. I also notice that the populations are going from highest to lowest. 
I wonder what causes most people to stick to certain areas. For example, most Indians are populated on the Northeastern coast and in California. This is also true for the Chinese population. I wonder if people are drawn to areas that already have high populations of their ethnic groups. I wonder if this is also because there are lots of opportunities on the coasts near larger cities. 
I relate to this graph because I am South Asian and this graph confirms what I have noticed for the Indian populations. I noticed this because my parents decided where they were living based on if it was diverse enough and that they could find an Indian community. 
Asian Populations On the Rise, But Only On the Coasts?

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

raw_comment:
- I noticed that when there are Asians in the west, it tends to be in large clumps. On the other hand, when there are Asians in the east, it tends to be in small dots. I also noticed that there are Japanese and Filipino people all over Hawaii.
- I wonder how different this graph looks two years later, in 2022. I also wonder why a lot of Asian people gravitate towards the west.
- This relates to me in numerous ways. As an Indian immigrant, I fit into this graph. My community is also made up of many other Indians. I wonder how different my life would be if I lived in a less diverse place.
- "Diversity's Becoming the Normality"

## 1) Chart type
**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

Visible group categories in the facets: **Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean, Japanese, Pakistani, Hmong, Cambodian, Thai, Laotian, Bangladeshi, Taiwanese, Burmese, Nepalese, Indonesian**.

**Faceted choropleth map / small-multiple thematic maps** of the United States.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: one U.S. map per Asian ethnic group.
- **No stacking**.
- Each panel uses the **same geographic base map** and highlights areas meeting a threshold.
- A shared legend indicates the highlighted regions represent places where the group is **at least 0.5% of total population**.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Asian group (e.g., Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | **Faceting** (separate map panel), **panel title text** |
| Geographic area within the U.S. (county/area location) | Spatial/geographic | **Position on map** |
| Whether the group makes up at least 0.5% of the local population | Quantitative threshold shown as binary condition | **Color/fill** of map areas (teal = meets threshold; unfilled/light = does not) |
| Total population of each group (e.g., 4.1 million, 771,000) | Quantitative | **Text label** beneath each panel title |

raw_comment:
I notice that there are many Asians along the West and East coast as well as a huge concentration around southern California spanning a lot of different subgroups of Asians. I also notice that for some groups, on the left half of the graph the areas where each group makes up at least 0.5%of the population are more clumpy and on the right half of the graph they seem more scattered about. I also find it interesting that there are more Filipino than Japanese and Koreans combined.

I wonder why there is such a big population of Asians in Southern California as well as the East Coast. I also wonder if eventually there will be more Indians than Chinese.

This graph relates to me and my community because as an Asian myself, I have lived in California, in a heavily Asian populated area all of my life and that makes me wonder what life would have been like if I had lived in a place where there are not as many Asians.

"Let's Start the Asian Population Conversation"

raw_comment:
First, I notice something that does not surprise me much: that there is a concentration of Asian populations on the West Coast -- specifically in the Los Angeles, Bay Area, and Seattle areas -- and to a lesser extent in New England in the east. I also notice, encouragingly, that these Asian populations in the United States are /everywhere/, all over the place, from Alaska to Utah to Texas to Maryland. I notice that the smaller groups are not often located in the Deep South, with some exceptions like Vietnamese famously South, Laotians in Louisiana and Thai folks in Mississippi. Numerically, I notice that the population numbers are /huge/, with millions and millions of Asian folks living across the Union.

I wonder about why there are concentrations of Asian populations in parts of the Southwest, like Southwest Texas, or Phoenix, or Southeastern Utah, of all places. I wonder why Hmong folks in California are mainly in the center, away from the famous coast. I wonder why there aren't big populations of more Asian groups in Hawaii. Maybe Hawaii is too expensive or does not carry enough economic promise? 

As a St. Louisan, I do not think our city is famous for its Asian populations. But as a Midwesterner, I am excited to see folks -- especially Filipinos -- across the Midwest. It also seems like Minnesota and Wisconsin are doing great to attract big populations. Overall, I get an impression of unity: "Asia is Our Ally: Asian Populations Extend Across the Entirety of the Union."

1. I notice that the Asian population of the United States is mostly concentrated on the west coast and a little bit on the east coast, similar to the concentration of the population, which makes sense. 
2. I wonder what caused the condensing of certain races in certain places - why are Cambodian people very concentrated in southeast Utah? Why are Filipinos and Japanese people so concentrated in Hawaii? Does this graphic include mixed race / part Asian people?

It's also interesting to see this especially during Covid, which has skyrocketed Asian hate and hate crimes against Asian people and has drawn nationwide attention.

raw_comment:
Asian explosion
 
As can be seen from the graph, the Asian population in the US is as high as 20 million, while the Chinese population in mainland China is as high as 4.1 million. In second place is India, with an estimated population of 4 million. While most Chinese still live in the West, Asian communities are increasingly established in the southern suburbs and rural Midwest. I wonder whether some ethnic minorities were among the first immigrants who were largely determined by chance. Immigrant families or individuals initially choose a certain place by accident, and then their relatives and friends often choose to go to the same place, taking full advantage of their ethnic social network, thereby reducing the risk cost of immigration. Because of this, the population distribution of ethnic minorities has a relatively fixed geographical distribution. It is related to me and my community a lot. First, I'm glad to see that Asians are more and more widely distributed in the United States today, because international students like me will have more and more choices in the future. Since the outbreak of COVID-19 last year, the situation of Asians in the United States has drawn attention as social and demographic dispersion has intensified in Europe and the United States. Last but not least, the increase in Asians is a feature of cultural integration. As the population explosion with wide area, and community with a shared future for mankind, cultures can be blended and innovated.
